content:
I’m curious where people think the major gaps in LLM-driven proof search currently are.

I've noticed that many AI mathematics rely on lottery pass@k metrics.

  1. Generate a lot of candidates
  2. Sample until one compiles
  3. Report whether at least one proof passed verification.

I believe that is useful for measuring raw proof generation capabilities, but I'm not convinced that is the right choice for long horizon mathematics or research grade formalization.

My current position is closer to verification-gated, step-by-step proof search:

  • decompose a target into explicit obligations;
  • verify each intermediate result before building on it;
  • preserve compiler diagnostics and failed proof shapes;
  • search the library before rebuilding infrastructure;
  • promote reusable lemmas;
  • track assumptions, dependencies, provenance, and statement changes;
  • replay the complete result in a clean environment.
  • Contribute upstream

Our recent work on the Cycle Double Cover formalization made this distinction concrete.

The final OpenAI theorem is compact, and a model such as GPT-5.6 can sometimes produce a large working Lean development without exposing much intermediate work. However, independently re-deriving and auditing the result required us to reconstruct many of the intermediate arguments explicitly.

We repeatedly encountered mathematical concepts that were standard informally but were not available in Mathlib in the exact form needed. This required proving intermediate lemmas around:

  • finite loopless multigraphs;
  • cuts and bridgelessness;
  • flows;
  • cubic expansion;
  • parity identities;
  • even-subgraph covers;
  • minimal nonempty even edge sets;
  • decomposition into cycles;
  • projection of covers between graph constructions.

Some of these were ordinary library gaps. Others were bridges between different definitions or proof representations. The final proof hides that infrastructure because the finished dependency graph has already been compressed into named declarations.

This raises a question:

If a model produces a valid final Lean proof, how much of the research process should still be preserved?

Some questions I would be interested in hearing opinions on:

  1. Is verifier-gated stepwise search the likely long-term architecture, or will end-to-end proof generation become reliable enough to dominate?
  2. Should pass@k remain the main metric, or should we also measure cost per verified theorem, reusable lemma, or discharged obligation?
  3. How much failed-attempt and diagnostic history should serious AI formalizations publish?
  4. How should systems distinguish genuine research progress from thousands of trivial compiled lemmas?
  5. What should the standard trust surface for AI-authored formal mathematics include?
  6. When a model fills a Mathlib gap during a proof, how should that result be extracted, generalized, reviewed, and upstreamed?
  7. Is a final kernel-checked proof object sufficient for publication, or should reproducible “show your work” standards become normal?
This topic was moved here from #AI authored projects > The future of automated proof search by Kevin Buzzard.

Vario said:

  1. Is verifier-gated stepwise search the likely long-term architecture, or will end-to-end proof generation become reliable enough to dominate?

I agree stepwise search is necessary:

Large, groundbreaking proofs (e.g. FLT) do not arise from a single, glorious QED. They arise from hundreds and hundreds of intermediate results. The Cycle Double Cover result is indeed impressive, but we should remember that the final proof is still a mere 3 pages long--it did not need to invent a whole new field of math to solve this problem.

One day, AI will start making progress on truly deep conjectures like RH, P=NP, Twin Prime, and it will need intermediate results. The grand unifying theory will be far too big to fit in a single agent's context window, so the only way to attack these problems will be to compartmentalize.

I agree with this 100%. I’m currently using verifier-gated automated proof search to formalize the Cycle Double Cover argument in Lean, and even Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 expanded into nearly 39 intermediate proof obligations.

Vario said:

Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 expanded into nearly 39 intermediate proof obligations.

The reality of formalization is that even small lemmas can be very tedious to prove if you do not yet have the background infrastructure. Mathlib tries to provide that foundation, but coverage is still low especially at research level.

The advantage of informal reasoning is that we can use intuition, concepts, "big picture" reasoning to move much more rapidly across the search space. I think a math-research loop could look like:

1) Fleet of informal agents read papers, articles, textbooks--then try to come up with reasonable conjectures based on existing literature. Report back only after one finds a novel proof.
2) Fleet of formalization agents translate the proof into Lean, provide surrounding API/infra/documentation to prep for future iterations building on top of that result.
